messages.author: 88be8046d498a27b
messages.subject: slowdown during gaussian process emulation of high-dimensional output from computer simulations
parts:
I am attempting to use STAN to model the high-dimensional output of a detailed, deterministic, black-box computer simulation L(x). I model L(x) as the linear combination of a set of basis functions (principal components), where the number of basis functions in the model is much less than dims(L(x)). For a given x, each basis function has a weight that is modeled as a gaussian process. The GP covariance matrices depend on x, the point at which the surrogate model is to be evaluated, and x_T, the points for which the full simulation has already been evaluated, and the realizations from the GP posteriors depend on coeffs_T, the principal component coefficients derived from the evaluations of x_T. This may be familiar to some as “gaussian process emulation,” following the work of Kennedy and O’Hagan (2001), and others.

For some observed L* I would like to use this model to infer the corresponding x*, via

L(x*) ~ normal(L*, L*_err);

where L*_err is observational error on L*.

A simplified version of my implementation of this model in STAN is attached. It compiles and runs, but the iteration completion time increases dramatically with increasing iteration number, while the time to execute the “model” block remains constant throughout. I can clock the time it takes the code to hit the end of the model block with a print statement. During execution, the final line of the model block is reached an average of 2 or 3 times a second per chain. For iterations < ~30 during the warmup phase, the frequency at which a chain completes an iteration is also about 2 or 3 per second. However, for iterations > ~30, tens of seconds, then minutes, then hours go by without an advance in the iteration number. As a consequence of this, I have never been able to get my model past the warmup phase (the highest iteration I ever let it hit was ~150 out of 2000, which took several hours). Results from the print statement at the end of the model block, however, continue to go by at 2 or 3 times a second, independent of iteration number.

Can anyone offer some advice on this issue? I also wonder if I have implemented my model, specifically the GP realizations, as efficiently as possible.

Thanks in advance for your help,

Danny

messages.author: a5e83218c834e013
messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] slowdown during gaussian process emulation of high-dimensional output from computer simulations
parts:
When you put together “high-dimesional output” and “gaussian process emulation”
you should get very, very scared.

The problem is that in high-dimensions Gaussian process emulation does not
work particularly well unless you have _lots_ of points.  And by lots I mean
a number that grows exponentially with the size of dimension.  When you
don’t have enough points then you run into the problem that the GP isn’t 
sufficiently regularized — there are an exponentially growing number of
functions that interpolate between the given points equally well.

The consequence for doing full Bayes is that the posterior in this case is
_nasty_.  Just crazy nasty.  What’s likely happening is that the adaptation
quickly moves towards a really small step size and NUTS then moves
towards a huge number of leapfrog steps to maintain a reasonable
exploration and drives up the computation time accordingly (note that
print statements are evaluated at each leapfrog step, so if you have
a huge number of steps you’ll still see lots of print statements without
necessarily any advance to the next iteration).

Others might suggest otherwise, but I’ll firmly say to not try to use
GP emulation (or really any emulation) in high dimensions!

messages.author: 88be8046d498a27b
messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] slowdown during gaussian process emulation of high-dimensional output from computer simulations
parts:
Hi Michael,

Thanks for your feedback.

Although the output of the computer simulation is high-dimensional (len(L) ~ 120, len(x) = 5), the dimensionality of the space in which realizations are drawn from the emulator is smaller by ~an order of magnitude or more due to the use of basis functions to represent L. In this particular problem, the reduced order model for L is just a sum over a truncated PCA basis, where the PCs are derived from evaluations of the full simulation at many x, designed to fill parameter space, and each coefficient is associated with an independent GP:

L_emulated(x) = \Sum_i^N pc_coeffs[i] * pc_component[i]
pc_coeffs[i] ~ GP(0, Sigma[i]);

The dimensionality of pc_component[i] is equal to the dimensionality of L. Using N=3, we only have to train 3 GPs, to predict coefficients for 3 PCs, but we can capture ~95% of the variance in the 700 instance training sample.

Originally I was using N=15, which is still quite a few GPs to train and may lend itself to the nasty posteriors you mentioned. However, for the sake of example, if I reduce the size of my PCA basis to only N=2 components with 200 training examples (a low-dimensional, well-conditioned space in my particular problem), I experience similar sampling times and a similar slowdown of the advancement of the iterations as I did when making realizations in the 15 dimensional space. I find this to be pretty confusing as the emulator is just realizing scalars from the posterior predictive distributions of 2 GPs and fitting a number of nuisance hyperparameters.

I’ll note that gaussian process reduced order models have been applied successfully as emulators for the high-dimensional outputs of computer simulations over the years, in several different fields. Many of these applications include the implementation of fully bayesian inference for x* using MCMC.

http://amstat.tandfonline.com/doi/abs/10.1198/016214507000000888
http://arxiv.org/pdf/1412.5177v1.pdf

Danny

messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] slowdown during gaussian process emulation of high-dimensional output from computer simulations
parts:
Hi Seth,

Yes, the original model I sent out should have f --> y. Attached is a model that implements this change as well as the new priors. I have also attached two data sets, one that uses a truncated PCA basis of size N=2 and another that uses a truncated PCA basis of size N=15. Running the model on both data sets should reveal similar slowdown behavior. The datasets are in the python format of a pickled dictionary of numpy arrays. To load a dataset and run it, you can use the following python code:

import pickle, pystan
data = pickle.load(open('em_data.N2.pkl','rb'))
result = pystan.stan(file='emulator.stan', data=data, refresh=1)


Note the refresh=1 keyword argument in the call to pystan.stan -- this is crucial for seeing the slowdown.

Danny

On Sunday, July 19, 2015 at 4:41:31 AM UTC-7, Seth Flaxman wrote:
Can you share some data so I can try running the model? Also, does
what you sent compile? On lines 132-134 should y be f?

Seth

On Sat, Jul 18, 2015 at 10:03 PM, Daniel Goldstein <da...@berkeley.edu> wrote:
> Hi Michael,
>
>
> Thanks for your feedback.
>
>
> Although the output of the computer simulation is high-dimensional (len(L) ~
> 120, len(x) = 5), the dimensionality of the space in which realizations are
> drawn from the emulator is smaller by ~an order of magnitude or more due to
> the use of basis functions to represent L. In this particular problem, the
> reduced order model for L is just a sum over a truncated PCA basis, where
> the PCs are derived from evaluations of the full simulation at many x,
> designed to fill parameter space, and each coefficient is associated with an
> independent GP:
>
>
> L_emulated(x) = \Sum_i^N pc_coeffs[i] * pc_component[i]
>
> pc_coeffs[i] ~ GP(0, Sigma[i]);
>
>
> The dimensionality of pc_component[i] is equal to the dimensionality of L.
> Using N=3, we only have to train 3 GPs, to predict coefficients for 3 PCs,
> but we can capture ~95% of the variance in the 700 instance training sample.
>
>
> Originally I was using N=15, which is still quite a few GPs to train and may
> lend itself to the nasty posteriors you mentioned. However, for the sake of
> example, if I reduce the size of my PCA basis to  only N=2 components with
> 200 training examples (a low-dimensional, well-conditioned space in my
> particular problem), I experience similar sampling times and a similar
> slowdown of the advancement of the iterations as I did when making
> realizations in the 15 dimensional space. I find this to be pretty confusing
> as the emulator is just realizing scalars from the posterior predictive
> distributions of 2 GPs and fitting a number of nuisance hyperparameters.
>
>
> I’ll note that gaussian process reduced order models have been applied
> successfully as emulators for the high-dimensional outputs of computer
> simulations over the years, in several different fields. Many of these
> applications include the implementation of fully bayesian inference for x*
> using MCMC.
>
>
> http://amstat.tandfonline.com/doi/abs/10.1198/016214507000000888
>
> http://arxiv.org/pdf/1412.5177v1.pdf
>
>
> Danny
>
>
> On Saturday, July 18, 2015 at 4:53:48 PM UTC-7, Michael Betancourt wrote:
>>
>> When you put together “high-dimesional output” and “gaussian process
>> emulation”
>> you should get very, very scared.
>>
>> The problem is that in high-dimensions Gaussian process emulation does not
>> work particularly well unless you have _lots_ of points.  And by lots I
>> mean
>> a number that grows exponentially with the size of dimension.  When you
>> don’t have enough points then you run into the problem that the GP isn’t
>> sufficiently regularized — there are an exponentially growing number of
>> functions that interpolate between the given points equally well.
>>
>> The consequence for doing full Bayes is that the posterior in this case is
>> _nasty_.  Just crazy nasty.  What’s likely happening is that the
>> adaptation
>> quickly moves towards a really small step size and NUTS then moves
>> towards a huge number of leapfrog steps to maintain a reasonable
>> exploration and drives up the computation time accordingly (note that
>> print statements are evaluated at each leapfrog step, so if you have
>> a huge number of steps you’ll still see lots of print statements without
>> necessarily any advance to the next iteration).
>>
>> Others might suggest otherwise, but I’ll firmly say to not try to use
>> GP emulation (or really any emulation) in high dimensions!
>>
>> On Jul 18, 2015, at 11:10 PM, Daniel Goldstein <da...@berkeley.edu> wrote:
>>
>> I should also note that memory usage is quite stable for the duration of
>> the warmup phase, independent of iteration number. If one does a `top` on
>> the machine where the code is running, the result is basically as follows,

>> 26842 dgold     20   0  454m 123m  36m R    100  0.0  11:58.82 python
>> 26841 dgold     20   0  454m 123m  36m R     99  0.0  11:57.99 python
>> 26845 dgold     20   0  454m 123m  36m R     99  0.0  11:57.95 python
>>
>> Danny
>>
>> On Saturday, July 18, 2015 at 2:36:31 PM UTC-7, Daniel Goldstein wrote:
>>>
>>> I am attempting to use STAN to model the high-dimensional output of a
>>> detailed, deterministic, black-box computer simulation L(x). I model L(x) as
>>> the linear combination of a set of basis functions (principal components),
>>> where the number of basis functions in the model is much less than
>>> dims(L(x)). For a given x, each basis function has a weight that is modeled
>>> as a gaussian process. The GP covariance matrices depend on x, the point at
>>> which the surrogate model is to be evaluated, and x_T, the points for which
>>> the full simulation has already been evaluated, and the realizations from
>>> the GP posteriors depend on coeffs_T, the principal component coefficients
>>> derived from the evaluations of x_T. This may be familiar to some as
>>> “gaussian process emulation,” following the work of Kennedy and O’Hagan
>>> (2001), and others.
>>>
>>>
>>> For some observed L* I would like to use this model to infer the
>>> corresponding x*, via
>>>
>>>
>>> L(x) ~ normal(L*, L*_err);
>>>
>>>
>>> where L*_err is observational error on L*.
>>>
>>>
>>> A simplified version of my implementation of this model in STAN is
>>> attached. It compiles and runs, but  the iteration completion time increases
>>> dramatically with increasing iteration number, while the time to execute the
>>> “model” block remains constant throughout. I can clock the time it takes the
>>> code to hit the end of the model block with a print statement. During
>>> execution, the final line of the model block is reached an average of 2 or 3
>>> times a second per chain. For iterations < ~30 during the warmup phase, the
>>> frequency at which  a chain completes an iteration is also about 2 or 3 per
>>> second. However, for iterations > ~30, tens of seconds, then minutes, then
>>> hours go by without an advance in the iteration number. As a consequence of
>>> this, I have never been able to get my model past the warmup phase (the
>>> highest iteration I ever let it hit was ~150 out of 2000, which took several
>>> hours). Results from the print statement at the end of the model block,
>>> however, continue to go by at 2 or 3 times a second, independent of
>>> iteration number.
>>>
>>>
>>> Can anyone offer some advice on this issue? I also wonder if I have
>>> implemented my model, specifically the GP realizations, as efficiently as
>>> possible.
>>>
>>>
>>> Thanks in advance for your help,
>>>
>>> Danny
>>
